The second batch of paraformaldehyde was added at 10 h when 100 mM formaldehyde was converted to GA. While the addition of 25 mM paraformaldehyde resulted in a slight improvement in GA titer compared to no addition, cells could not handle 50 mM addition, resulting in the accumulation of formaldehyde 43 concentrations and slowdown of the activity (Figure 29E). ACR: acyl-CoA reductase; EcAldA: 2-hydroxyaldehyde dehydrogenase from E. coli; and TE: endogenous thioesterases. (D) Overview of titer (green bar), pH (pink bar), and yield (in % carbon above graphs) at 24 h for four different conditions tested. Prototyping the bioconversion pathway of formate to ethylene glycol (Task 10) 44 USF utilized in vitro pathway prototyping to evaluate the entire pathway and demonstrate ethylene glycol production from formate. For this, enzymes that had been previously identified and characterized for formaldehyde and formyl-CoA condensation (RuHACLG390N), glycolyl-CoA reduction (LmACR), and glycolaldehyde reduction (FucO) were combined in a reaction system which also included enzymes for formyl- CoA and formaldehyde generation from formate. For the latter, a transferase (OfFrc) utilizing succinyl-CoA as the CoA donor for formate to formyl-CoA conversion was used in conjunction with LmACR, capable of reducing formyl-CoA to formaldehyde.
